query: Write a founder video ad for an ecommerce product with proof and a purchase CTA

cards.title: Highest-performing founder ad script structure: claim, proof, mechanism, CTA
cards.summary: Use the Claim → Proof of Claim → Unique Mechanism (founder story) → Proof of Mechanism → CTA/Social Proof sequence identified from top-spending founder ads.
cards.use_when: Drafting the body script for a founder video ad for cold acquisition traffic.
steps: Open with an adversarial claim that doubles as a hook, e.g. 'the industry is lying about X' or 'big supermarkets sell you Y that is full of plastic'.
Immediately prove the claim — the source found no top performer that made a claim without proof. Example framing: 'a study found competitors contain 1/100 of the stated ingredient'.
Move into the unique mechanism tied to the founder story: the adversarial problem existed, competitors did the bad thing, so the founder built the differentiated solution.
Layer more proof onto the mechanism (factory visits, third-party testing, ingredient labels, certificates) so the viewer believes the mechanism is real.
Close with the CTA — how to buy, the offer, scarcity and urgency — plus customer social proof.
Keep the CTA simple: average watch time means few viewers reach it, so the source does not bother testing multiple CTAs on the same body.
caveats: This structure was the top performer among the source's own top-spending founder ads in their ad account; it is a source-specific finding, not a universal ranking.
Adversarial competitor claims carry compliance and legal risk — the source notes founders are often more willing than agencies to take that risk.
cards.source_name: How To Create Founder Ads That Scale (Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Highest-Performing Founder Script Structure
cards.summary: The source's strongest founder script sequence runs Claim, Proof of Claim, Unique Mechanism tied to founder story, Proof of Mechanism, CTA plus social proof.
cards.use_when: Writing or reviewing the body script for a founder-led video ad before shooting.
steps: Open with an adversarial claim that challenges the viewer's assumptions about the category (the source's example: 'the industry is lying to you'). This creates tension before the product is introduced.
Immediately provide proof of that claim so the adversarial opening reads as credible rather than inflammatory.
Introduce the unique mechanism tied to the founder's story — connect why the product works to why the founder built it.
Back the mechanism with proof of mechanism: evidence, demonstration, or results that validate the explanation.
End with a clear CTA plus social proof to close the loop on trust.
Run this as the body script, then test multiple hooks in front of it rather than rewriting the whole structure per concept.
caveats: This is presented as the source's highest-performing founder structure, not a universal law; it depends on having a real adversarial claim and real proof to back it.
cards.source_name: How To Create Founder Ads That Scale (Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Sequence an Ad as Hook, Curiosity Gap, Objection Handling, Benefits
cards.summary: A strong founder ad can be built in a deliberate sequence: credibility hook, curiosity gap, warehouse social proof, objection handling, then benefits over features.
cards.use_when: Scripting a founder product ad for an ecommerce brand, especially a supplement or food product with a common objection.
steps: Open with a credibility hook that signals legitimacy — the example opens with the product having taken over two years of development.
Immediately open a curiosity gap (the example: 'and here's why') to pull the viewer forward before explaining anything.
Insert social proof visually as the founder walks through the warehouse, so the audience sees scale/operations while listening.
Bridge into objection handling: the example names every negative attribute of competing products ('gluggy, gritty, grainy, and gluey') before making any claim about his own.
Move to benefits instead of features — smooth and creamy, under 1g of sugar, budget-friendly — after objections have been cleared.

Name the product only after the problem and benefits are established, and keep the CTA from opening new curiosity loops the ad then never closes (the source criticizes 'forget everything you know about pea protein' because it bridges nowhere).
caveats: The source flags the re-opened curiosity gap and the CTA as weaknesses in this otherwise strong ad — do not copy them.
No performance numbers are given; this is a structural commentary, not a tested result.
cards.source_name: How To Create Founder Ads That Scale (Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Sequencing Proof Before Product Reveal
cards.summary: A premium toothbrush ad front-loads a founder story and problem agitation and delays the product reveal, letting low-fi founder footage contrast with premium product shots.
cards.use_when: Creating acquisition video for a premium-positioned product where you want to justify the price before showing the product.
steps: Open by building authority through the founder's credentials (time spent in dental labs) and then state a category-level claim the big brands 'hope you never notice'.

Build stakes with a concrete, quantified research story: they bought every top-rated electric toothbrush, spent thousands of dollars on name brands with celebrity ads and $300 price tags, and used them for months.

Agitate on the discovered problems — porous plastic absorbing bathroom moisture, charging bases acting like Petri dishes collecting black mould where the brush is stored, Bluetooth apps added to justify markup — before any product is shown.

Reveal the solution only after agitation, with specific materials and spec choices (aircraft-grade aluminum vice plastic, 14 motor frequencies tested to settle on 32,000 micro-vibrations per minute, wall mount instead of countertop stand, 60-day battery).

Use the contrast deliberately: the source notes low-fi founder footage early does not damage a premium brand as long as the product is not introduced in that lower-quality footage — it creates contrast with the later high-end product shots.
Close on the positioning line and a comparison CTA inviting the viewer to upgrade from a name brand that stopped caring.
caveats: The claim that low-fi footage is safe 'as long as the product isn't introduced at the same time' is the presenter's reasoning, not a tested result.
Volume of proof claims must be legally defensible; the source gives no guidance on substantiation.
cards.source_name: How To Create Founder Ads That Scale (Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Founder Ad = Founder's Argument, Not Raw Footage
cards.summary: A founder ad is a structured presentation of the founder's argument across three story elements, not simply video of the founder talking.
cards.use_when: Planning a founder-led ad concept for a Meta acquisition campaign and deciding what the ad actually needs to communicate.
steps: Treat the founder ad as a constructed argument rather than documentary footage of the founder. The source defines it as a structured presentation of the founder's case, not just a camera pointed at them.

Build the argument from three elements: the origin (why the business started), the unique mechanism (why the solution works, explained by the founder or an expert), and an adversarial angle (tearing down competitors or industry norms).
Anchor the origin to a real problem the founder encountered that maps to the customer's problem — this is what makes the authority credible rather than decorative.
Use the unique mechanism to explain why the product works differently, giving the founder or an expert the role of explaining the mechanism.
Use the adversarial angle to differentiate: name what the industry does wrong and position the product against it.
This framework suits founder-led brands where the founder has genuine category authority or a credible origin story. If the founder has neither, a witness or proxy format may fit better.
caveats: The source frames this as a definition and architecture, not a guaranteed performance formula; adversarial claims should be truthful and substantiated.
cards.source_name: How To Create Founder Ads That Scale (Masterclass).docx

query: Plan static ad concepts around product personas awareness and landing page fit

cards.title: Concept = Persona × Angle × Offer × Format
cards.summary: A true static ad concept is the intersection of persona, angle, offer and format; anything less is usually an immeasurable variation.
cards.use_when: Planning a static ad test batch for your store and deciding which changes count as new concepts versus minor design tweaks.
steps: Define four slots for every concept: who it's for (persona), the persuasive angle, the offer, and the format (native, advertorial, before/after, listicle, feature call-out).
Only count a new ad as a new concept when at least one of those four elements genuinely changes.

Discard or deprioritize tests that only change a background color, font, or minor layout — the source argues these are grouped by Meta's algorithm (Andromeda) under the same Entity ID, so no real learning is produced.
Keep a concept grid so your team can see coverage gaps — e.g., many angles for one persona but no offers for another.
Prioritize concept breadth over polish depth when planning the week's output.
caveats: The Andromeda Entity ID grouping is the source's explanation of Meta's current behavior; verify against the current Meta interface and documentation as it evolves.
Some minor visual refinement still matters for a finished ad — the point is not to count it as a separate test.
cards.source_name: How to Make Static Image Ads That Scale in 2026.docx

cards.title: Format-to-Awareness Map for Static Ad Planning
cards.summary: Use a rough map of static formats by funnel stage to decide which formats to test at the top, middle and bottom of the funnel.
cards.use_when: Building a static ad test plan across funnel stages or filling gaps in a creative testing calendar.
steps: Top of funnel formats: problem agitation statics, native statics, PR/advertorial statics, founder statics (photo of founder doing something, either very curious or very clear).
Middle of funnel formats: comparison ads, before-and-afters, listicles, feature call-outs (where most people default).
Bottom of funnel formats: offer call-outs, reviews, hero product shots.
Note from the source that most people's statics cluster in the middle and bottom, neglecting the top-of-funnel formats that reach cold audiences.
Test across stages rather than only in the account's comfort zone; find which format works, then scale it by rotating a concept element.
Use top-of-funnel formats with long-form primary text or educational landing pages to close the awareness gap.
caveats: Format alone is the least important variable, per the source; the concept (persona, angle, offer) matters more. Do not chase formats without a concept.
cards.source_name: How to Make Static Image Ads That Scale in 2026.docx

cards.title: Match Static Ad Format to Stage of Awareness
cards.summary: Most brands fail top-of-funnel by running product-aware or most-aware statics to cold, unaware audiences — instead lead cold traffic with education or problem agitation.
cards.use_when: Choosing which static ad concepts to produce for a cold prospecting campaign versus a retargeting campaign.
steps: Classify each concept by Eugene Schwartz awareness stage before producing it: most-aware/product-aware statics (plain product shots, 'guaranteed energy in 5 minutes') belong in retargeting, while unaware/problem-aware audiences need statics that lead with education or a named problem.
For cold audiences, open with a problem the viewer recognises rather than the product: the GLP-1 hair loss static leads with 'GLP1 hair loss hits hard' and only then introduces the supplement.
Use advertorial-style statics (native statics that look like content) to educate before the hard sell, since they let you agitate the problem without immediately demanding a purchase.

Check the mismatch symptom: a clean product shot with a benefit headline running against cold traffic is the format-audience mismatch the source names as the primary reason top-of-funnel statics fail.
Route each stage to the right destination — education/curiosity concepts need an educational landing page, while product-aware concepts can go to a standard PDP.
caveats: Awareness stages are used as a strategist's organising framework here; the source offers no measurement data linking stage to ROAS, so treat the alignment as a planning discipline rather than a proven lift.
cards.source_name: How To Make Better Meta Ads_ 8 Static Creatives Analysed.docx

cards.title: Align Ad Concept to the Five Stages of Awareness
cards.summary: Use Eugene Schwartz's five stages of awareness (unaware, problem aware, solution aware, product aware, most aware) to match static ad concepts to the correct audience temperature.
cards.use_when: Mapping your store's static ad concepts to cold, warm, or retargeting audiences and diagnosing why a static ad underperforms.
steps: Classify each ad concept by the awareness stage it assumes: does it presume the viewer knows the problem, the solution category, your product, or just your brand?
Check the audience you're targeting against that assumption — a plain product shot presumes product/most-aware audiences.
For cold, unaware traffic, use curiosity-driven native statics that name a problem or provoke interest, not product showcases.
Build a funnel map showing at least one concept per awareness stage so the account covers the full path, not just bottom-funnel retargeting.
Diagnose underperformance by asking whether the ad was served to an audience below its assumed awareness stage.
caveats: The source identifies a mismatch — deploying most-aware/product-aware assets to cold unaware audiences — as the primary reason static ads fail to scale; treat this as its stated diagnosis, not a controlled finding.
Stage labels are qualitative heuristics, not measurable audience segments in the ad platform.
cards.source_name: How to Make Static Image Ads That Scale in 2026.docx

cards.title: Persona Callout Static for Problem-Aware Audiences (GLP-1 Template)
cards.summary: Lead a static with a specific persona label and recognizable object, then widen into a curiosity gap about a solution rather than naming the product.
cards.use_when: Writing a static ad targeting a clearly defined, problem-aware audience segment where a specific identifier is instantly recognizable.
steps: Open with the persona in the headline — the source cites 'GLP-1' as a single term that instantly signals the audience is seen.
Validate the callout with a universally recognizable visual for that audience (e.g. an insulin injection pen) so the ad feels like it's for insiders.
Introduce a tension or negation ('without the side effects') and list the specific pains — gut discomfort, energy, hair, skin — to trigger problem awareness.
Present a broad solution category ('clinical-grade nutritional support', 'the complete GLP-1 companion') without specifying the product — the source deliberately keeps this broad to generate a click.
Send the click to a long-form educational landing page that resolves the open loop; do not route this static straight to a product page.
caveats: The source warns this ad type fails on a product page — the education step is not optional.
Referring to prescription drug names or claims may trigger platform and regulatory review; verify compliance for your category and geography.
No performance data was shared for the cited example.
cards.source_name: How to Make Static Image Ads That Scale in 2026.docx

query: Test new hooks for a fatigued product video while keeping the winning body

cards.title: Revive a Fatigued Hero Ad by Replacing Only the Hook
cards.summary: A proven testimonial ad that fatigued after months can be revitalized by attaching new 3-5 second hooks rather than discarding the asset.
cards.use_when: A previously top-performing video ad (e.g. testimonial) has fatigued after extended spend and stopped scaling.
steps: Confirm the ad is genuinely fatigued: in the source's example a top performer that ran roughly six to seven months and was about 5x better than anything else began to lose results.
Instead of filming entirely new concepts, rework only the first 3-5 seconds of the proven body.
Avoid simply repurposing more hooks from the existing footage; most of your market already saw that hook and dropped off, so reuse of the same avatar/visual rarely re-engages them.
Shoot new hooks with a different person, e.g. EGC (Employee Generated Content) delivering the hook before transitioning into the original CGC (Customer Generated Content) testimonial body.
In the source's case this restored performance to prior levels at the same daily spend, and the reworked ads became the account's current top performers.
Treat these results as one account's example, not a guaranteed outcome; test your own winner before scaling spend assumptions.
caveats: The source could not show the actual client ad, so the performance figures are uncorroborated.
Results cited (5x, six-to-seven-month fatigue, restored spend) are specific to one account and not benchmarks.
cards.source_name: Why Hook Testing Still Works With Andromeda.docx

cards.title: Test More Than Three Hooks to Beat the Odds
cards.summary: Testing only two or three hook variations per concept has low odds of producing a winner; run many variations on a proven body instead.
cards.use_when: Choosing how many hook variations to produce when revitalizing a proven winning ad.
steps: Reject the trap of limiting variations out of fear that Andromeda will group them all together; that fear can push you to under-test.

If you test only an angle change and a couple of avatar changes (the source's example of three hooks), the odds of a high performer are low unless you are an exceptional scriptwriter with deep audience knowledge.
Instead produce a higher volume of hooks on the proven body; in the source's example they ran four different hooks across two bodies, reworking both hooks and body slightly.

Budget the work so the volume is achievable: making 10 versions of a 3-5 second hook is roughly the same effort as producing one ~75-second ad body, since most shooting and editing effort lives in the body.
Because the hook drives retention, concentrate repeated low-effort iterations there while keeping the proven body intact.
caveats: The claim that 'three hooks is usually too few' is the source's heuristic, not a calculated benchmark.
The 10-versions-equal-one-body effort comparison is the source's practical estimate for their own 75-second format.
cards.source_name: Why Hook Testing Still Works With Andromeda.docx

cards.title: Don't Abandon Hook Testing Because of Andromeda
cards.summary: Andromeda may group near-identical ads but rotating substantially different hooks still unlocks net-new reach for fatigued winners, so hook testing remains high-value.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to keep testing hooks on a fatigued winning ad or to kill it and start entirely new creative concepts.
steps: Recognize the widespread claim that Andromeda groups minor variations into single Entity IDs and therefore punishes hook testing; the source argues this leads advertisers to a mistake.
Understand that Andromeda groups visually and contextually identical ads, not every variation of a hook; the source maintains hook testing still works on live accounts.
Agree that diverse creative has always been valuable, but don't let that reasoning cancel the hook's outsized importance in paid social video.
Because the hook sells the ad, the source places roughly 90% of a creative's impact in the first 3-5 seconds, citing Ogilvy's headline logic.
Continue running hook variations on proven bodies as your default low-effort, high-ROI play rather than only producing entirely new assets.
Verify current Meta/Andromeda behavior on your own account rather than assuming the algorithm has made hook testing obsolete, because tool behavior can change.
caveats: This is the source's opinion and account experience, not a documented platform rule; confirm with your own tests.
Andromeda grouping behavior may change over time, so re-validate the assumption on live campaigns.
cards.source_name: Why Hook Testing Still Works With Andromeda.docx

cards.title: Hook Testing Still Works Post-Andromeda
cards.summary: Test new openings as low-cost refinements of existing product-ad concepts and measure their purchase impact.
cards.use_when: When deciding whether to invest in hook variation under Meta's Andromeda-era diversity expectations.
steps: Create hook variants while keeping the body stable. A changed opening does not by itself prove that delivery will reach a new audience.
Accept overlap risk: because most of the body is identical, the concept is the same, so treat hook swaps as refinements of one concept, not new concepts.
Do it because the effort is nearly free: recording hooks six times takes minutes.

Revive fatigued winners: the source reports ads that spent $50,000-$100,000 then fatigued, and rotating 50 new hooks yielded another $100,000 of spend at the same efficiency from roughly one hour of shooting.
Revive losers with a bad hook rate by fixing only the hook, keeping the rest of the asset.
Treat hooks as the highest-leverage point across video, organic and YouTube, per the source.
caveats: The $50k-$100k figures are the source's own case examples, not guaranteed results.
Andromeda behavior may change; verify current platform behavior.
cards.source_name: The Creative Strategy Behind $100M_yr of Meta Spend.docx

cards.title: Hook is the highest-leverage test in a VSL
cards.summary: Because roughly 80% of viewers drop off before the body script starts, test 3–6 hook variations against a fixed body and CTA rather than rewriting everything.
cards.use_when: Improving performance of an already-produced VSL, or structuring a paid social test plan for a long-form video ad.
steps: Build the body of the VSL (problem, mechanism, proof, CTA) first, then produce 3–6 competing hooks against that same body.
Test the hooks as the primary variable rather than rewriting the entire script each time.

Do not bridge immediately into brand or product after the hook—transition into the Problem phase with educational problem-agitation (e.g., explain the biological cause of tooth decay) so viewers stay engaged and don't realize early that it's an ad.

Match hook relevance to audience: the source's strong examples open with content specific to who has the problem (e.g., 'people with tonsil stones'), which filters in the right viewer and lets others self-select out.
Keep the CTA on the main asset if this is your first VSL rather than splitting it into a separate retargeting asset.
caveats: The 80% drop-off figure is the source's stated figure, not a measured benchmark.
The source says many VSLs perform better with older demographics, so readable, large text matters—unreadable text is an editor-level failure it calls out.

[c8317f1a229190bf06d2a0a9] Revive a Fatigued Hero Ad by Replacing Only the Hook
Use when: A previously top-performing video ad (e.g. testimonial) has fatigued after extended spend and stopped scaling.
- Confirm the ad is genuinely fatigued: in the source's example a top performer that ran roughly six to seven months and was about 5x better than anything else began to lose results.
- Instead of filming entirely new concepts, rework only the first 3-5 seconds of the proven body.
- Avoid simply repurposing more hooks from the existing footage; most of your market already saw that hook and dropped off, so reuse of the same avatar/visual rarely re-engages them.
- Shoot new hooks with a different person, e.g. EGC (Employee Generated Content) delivering the hook before transitioning into the original CGC (Customer Generated Content) testimonial body.
- In the source's case this restored performance to prior levels at the same daily spend, and the reworked ads became the account's current top performers.
- Treat these results as one account's example, not a guaranteed outcome; test your own winner before scaling spend assumptions.
Caveat: The source could not show the actual client ad, so the performance figures are uncorroborated.
Caveat: Results cited (5x, six-to-seven-month fatigue, restored spend) are specific to one account and not benchmarks.

[59cf922e49969510cdd411de] Test More Than Three Hooks to Beat the Odds
Use when: Choosing how many hook variations to produce when revitalizing a proven winning ad.
- Reject the trap of limiting variations out of fear that Andromeda will group them all together; that fear can push you to under-test.
- If you test only an angle change and a couple of avatar changes (the source's example of three hooks), the odds of a high performer are low unless you are an exceptional scriptwriter with deep audience knowledge.
- Instead produce a higher volume of hooks on the proven body; in the source's example they ran four different hooks across two bodies, reworking both hooks and body slightly.
- Budget the work so the volume is achievable: making 10 versions of a 3-5 second hook is roughly the same effort as producing one ~75-second ad body, since most shooting and editing effort lives in the body.
- Because the hook drives retention, concentrate repeated low-effort iterations there while keeping the proven body intact.
Caveat: The claim that 'three hooks is usually too few' is the source's heuristic, not a calculated benchmark.
Caveat: The 10-versions-equal-one-body effort comparison is the source's practical estimate for their own 75-second format.

[2d5a90d21b0dfb6e27fbf792] Don't Abandon Hook Testing Because of Andromeda
Use when: Deciding whether to keep testing hooks on a fatigued winning ad or to kill it and start entirely new creative concepts.
- Recognize the widespread claim that Andromeda groups minor variations into single Entity IDs and therefore punishes hook testing; the source argues this leads advertisers to a mistake.
- Understand that Andromeda groups visually and contextually identical ads, not every variation of a hook; the source maintains hook testing still works on live accounts.
- Agree that diverse creative has always been valuable, but don't let that reasoning cancel the hook's outsized importance in paid social video.
- Because the hook sells the ad, the source places roughly 90% of a creative's impact in the first 3-5 seconds, citing Ogilvy's headline logic.
- Continue running hook variations on proven bodies as your default low-effort, high-ROI play rather than only producing entirely new assets.
- Verify current Meta/Andromeda behavior on your own account rather than assuming the algorithm has made hook testing obsolete, because tool behavior can change.
Caveat: This is the source's opinion and account experience, not a documented platform rule; confirm with your own tests.
Caveat: Andromeda grouping behavior may change over time, so re-validate the assumption on live campaigns.

[2f44cbccd498fdfe8d9f9a82] Hook Testing Still Works Post-Andromeda
Use when: When deciding whether to invest in hook variation under Meta's Andromeda-era diversity expectations.
- Create hook variants while keeping the body stable. A changed opening does not by itself prove that delivery will reach a new audience.
- Accept overlap risk: because most of the body is identical, the concept is the same, so treat hook swaps as refinements of one concept, not new concepts.
- Do it because the effort is nearly free: recording hooks six times takes minutes.
- Revive fatigued winners: the source reports ads that spent $50,000-$100,000 then fatigued, and rotating 50 new hooks yielded another $100,000 of spend at the same efficiency from roughly one hour of shooting.
- Revive losers with a bad hook rate by fixing only the hook, keeping the rest of the asset.
- Treat hooks as the highest-leverage point across video, organic and YouTube, per the source.
Caveat: The $50k-$100k figures are the source's own case examples, not guaranteed results.

query: Plan a profitable Whatnot live auction show with inventory and starting bids

cards.title: Starting Bids at $1: When It Works and When It Doesn't
cards.summary: $1 starts create excitement only when the room is full; the source says most sellers should not use them.
cards.use_when: Deciding starting bid prices for auction inventory in a live-stream show.
steps: Reserve $1 starting bids for high-quality, recognizable items ($50–$150 resale value) — buyers ignore $1 starts on $5–$10 junk.
Only start at $1 if you expect a large, excited room; the source describes success with 300–500 concurrent viewers.
Publicize '$1 starts' in your advertising because it is a strong hook that drives bookmarks.
Accept the unpredictability: some $1-start items will sell below market and some far above; the source calls this the inherent nature of $1 auctions.
For normal shows without a big promoted audience, start higher — the source explicitly does not recommend $1 starts for most sellers.
caveats: The recommendation to avoid $1 starts for most sellers is the presenter's opinion, tied to room size.
No guaranteed price floor exists; losses on individual items are expected.

cards.title: Live Auction Show Planning: Schedule Early, Promote Hard
cards.summary: Schedule live auction shows at least a week ahead and promote across channels to maximize bookmarks, which drives viewer turnout and higher average selling price.
cards.use_when: Planning a live-stream selling event (Whatnot or similar live auction) and deciding how far in advance to schedule and how to promote it.
steps: Schedule the show at least one week ahead, and two to three weeks out if possible, so the platform can remind bookmarked users when you go live.
Advertise the scheduled show on every channel you have: personal Facebook page, reseller Facebook groups, Instagram stories, and your YouTube videos.
Post promotion multiple times with escalating urgency: roughly one week before, two to three days before, and a few hours before the show.
Center the pre-show message on the quality of inventory and a reason to show up (for example 'high-quality inventory, all starting at $1'), not just the date.
Track bookmarks and max concurrent viewers as your feedback signal — the source's 530 max concurrent viewers (top-10 show in three years) was attributed to this multi-channel promotion.
caveats: The source's link between bookmarks and higher ASP is the seller's own experience, not a platform benchmark.
The presenter acknowledges their existing YouTube following helped; they also state sellers with no prior social following can grow purely inside the app.
cards.source_name: Our Secret Strategies to Making $975_Hour on Whatnot!.docx

cards.title: Pacing a High-Volume Auction Show
cards.summary: Budget ~45 seconds to 1 minute per item and expect a 250-item show to run close to 4 hours.
cards.use_when: Planning show length, item count, and staffing for a live auction event.
steps: Estimate time per lot: the source's 252 items took 3 hours 57 minutes, roughly 45 seconds to 1 minute each.
Set a minimum countdown (their auctions start at 15 seconds) but let bids extend the timer when bidding continues.
Account for your own talking time — the source's show ran longer than planned (2.5–3 hours expected, ~4 actual) because of extended commentary and 'soap boxes'.
Plan capacity accordingly: staff shipping/replenishment so orders from a big show can be processed afterward (their helper took ~2 days, 6–7 paid hours at $25/hour).
Use the time-per-item figure to sanity-check whether a target item count is realistic for your show length.
caveats: Time per item is the source's own observed average, not a platform standard.
Sellers who talk more or less will see different totals.
cards.source_name: Our Secret Strategies to Making $975_Hour on Whatnot!.docx

cards.title: Run a fast auction cadence (5-second bids, low starts)
cards.summary: Top live sellers run auctions in seconds at low opening prices, which converts browsing traffic into fast impulse purchases.
cards.use_when: Setting auction duration and starting price for items in a live-selling show.
steps: Observe top sellers in your category: the source's example ran 5-second auctions starting at $5.
Keep bidding friction minimal — viewers tap and swipe to bid, so the whole action takes about 2 seconds; do not add steps.
Start auctions at the price you actually want. If you want $20, start at $20; starting at $1 and resenting the outcome is a setup for conflict with buyers.
Never show frustration at low winning bids — buyers feel the attitude and leave for a more fun, more appreciative seller.

Use the buyer appreciation giveaway once you have regular attendance (the source suggests 20-40 regular viewers) to make mediocre items easier to move: buying anything enters the buyer into a draw for a strong prize at the end.
Check the math: extra revenue from the small items typically covers the cost of the giveaway prize.
caveats: The 5-second/$5 format is one top seller's observed setup, not a mandated format.
Buyer appreciation giveaways are advised only after you have a stable audience, not at launch.
cards.source_name: How to Start Selling on Whatnot with No Followers.docx

cards.title: Build Inventory Cheap to Protect Auction Margins
cards.summary: Source product from thrift bins, flea markets, and lot deals to keep COGS low enough that even $8–$15 sales are profitable.
cards.use_when: Sourcing inventory for a live auction or resale channel where per-item prices are low and volume is high.
steps: Buy from low-cost sources: thrift-store bins, flea markets, and bulk lots; the source buys at $0.25–$5 per item.
Look for bulk lot opportunities from other sellers — the source's friend offered 67 Funko Pops for $250 (~$4 per pop), which they considered a good deal.
Reuse already-paid-off inventory from previous events as effectively free cost of goods for the next show.
Aim for a consistent multiplier: the source targets roughly tripling money on low-cost items ($2 in, ~$8+ out) and relies on volume (about 150 items a week) for profitability.
Keep the show's total inventory cost low enough that break-even comes early — the source's $1,000-in / $1,000-out break-even for a 250-item show.
caveats: Low-cost sourcing is labor-intensive and depends on local supply; margins on tiny items are thin until moved at volume.
The source's sourcing channels (Goodwill bins, flea markets) are their own; other sources may yield different costs.
